title: The Ten Perfections for Little (p. 1–15)

Ten Perfections Little · Children’s Books

The Ten Perfections for Little (p. 1–15)

Pages 1–15 (15 pages)
Page 1

The Ten Perfections for Little Readers Ten good things the Buddha made perfect, with Sumedha's pictures and the old stories, told for children of about seven “Na sasassa tilā atthi, na muggā napi taṇḍulā; iminā agginā pakkaṃ, mamaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”: The hare has no sesame, no beans and no rice. Eat me, cooked on this fire, and live on in the forest. (Jātaka 316) Every Pali word is followed by its English in brackets. A quiz follows every two chapters; the answers are at the back. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 1

Page 3

How to read this book This book is for Anna, who is seven, and for other children of about that age. A child can read it alone, or an older person can read it aloud, a chapter at a time. It tells about ten good things. The Buddha made each of them perfect, in many, many lives, before he became the Buddha. The old books call them the ten pāramī (perfections). Where this book began. This book was inspired by The Perfections Leading to Enlightenment by Sujin Boriharnwanaket, translated by Nina van Gorkom, a book about the ten perfections for grown-ups. Her book draws on the old Pali books, and this one goes to the same old books for its stories and its Pali lines. There is a bigger book for older children, The Ten Perfections for Young Readers, that follows her book closely. Pali words. The Buddha’s words were kept in a language called Pali. Some Pali words are in this book. Every time one comes, its English is next to it in brackets, like this: dāna (giving). You do not have to remember the Pali to understand the page. But if you do remember some, you will know real words from the Buddha’s own books. Saying the words. A line over a letter makes it long. ā sounds like the “a” in “father”. ī sounds like the “ee” in “see”. ū sounds like the “oo” in “moon”. A dot under a letter (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) means the tongue curls back a little. ñ sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”. ṃ sounds like “ng”. So paññā is said “pan-nyaa” and mettā is said “met-taa”. The lines under the pictures. Under every picture there is a line in Pali from the Buddha’s own books, and after it the meaning in plain English. The Pali is exactly as it stands in the old books. The English was written for this book, and the name of the old book is given at the end of the line. Hard words. Some English words in this book are hard. The first time a hard word is met in a chapter it has a small number after it, like this: hermit³. Its meaning is given at the end of the chapter, under “Hard words in this chapter”, and all the hard words are listed together at the back, after the word list. In the web edition, tapping or clicking on the word shows its meaning. Quizzes. After every two chapters there is a short quiz. Where the stories come from. All the stories are old. The story of Sumedha comes from the Buddhavaṃsa (the Story of the Buddhas). The other stories come from the Jātaka (birth stories) and the Cariyāpiṭaka (Basket of Conduct). All three are books of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets), the oldest collection of the Buddha’s teaching. The Buddha told these stories himself. In each one he is the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be), the one who is working, life after life, to become a Buddha. The last pages of this book say where each story is found. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 3

Page 4

Introduction. Sumedha finds the ten “Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā; sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, santāressaṃ sadevakaṃ”: What good is it for me to cross over alone, a man who knows his own strength? I will reach full knowledge and carry the whole world across. (Buddhavaṃsa 2) Long, long ago there was a young man named Sumedha. He was very rich. But he saw that everyone gets old, everyone gets ill, and everyone dies. He did not want to go round and round in that for ever. So he gave away all his riches and went to live in the mountains. There he trained his mind until it was calm and strong. At that time there was a Buddha in the world. His name was Dīpaṅkara. One day Sumedha heard that the Buddha Dīpaṅkara was coming to a town nearby. The people were making the road smooth for him. Sumedha asked for a piece of the road to make smooth too. But before he had finished, the Buddha came. There was still mud on Sumedha’s piece of road. So Sumedha lay down in the mud. He spread his long hair over it. He thought: let the Buddha and his monks1 walk over me, so that their feet do not touch the mud. As he lay there, Sumedha knew that he could end all his own troubles that very day, if he wished. But he thought: what good is it to cross over alone? I will become a Buddha myself, and I will carry the whole world across. The Buddha Dīpaṅkara stood by his head. He said to the people: this man will become a Buddha. His name will be Gotama. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 4

Page 5

The ten. Then Sumedha asked himself: what does a person need, to become a Buddha? He looked, and he found ten things. He found them one by one, and for each one he thought of a picture. The first was dāna (giving). Then came sīla (good conduct), nekkhamma (letting go), paññā (wisdom), viriya (energy2), khanti (patience), sacca (truthfulness3), adhiṭṭhāna (determination4), mettā (loving-kindness5) and upekkhā (even-mindedness6). These are the ten pāramī (perfections7). This book has one chapter for each of them, and each chapter tells Sumedha’s picture for it. A pāramī (perfection) is a good thing made as big and as strong as it can be. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) made all ten perfect. It took him a time so long that nobody can count it: four uncountable ages and a hundred thousand ages more. This shore kilesa (defilements) wanting anger ignorance Far shore nibbāna (the end of all troubles) peace dāna giving sīla good conduct nekkhamma letting go paññā wisdom viriya energy khanti patience sacca truthfulness adhiṭṭhāna determination mettā loving-kindness upekkhā even mind “Sabbe dhammā anattā ti, yadā paññāya passati; atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā”: All things are not self. When a person sees this with wisdom, he turns away from suffering. This is the path to purity. (Dhammapada 279) The old teachers also say that the word pāramī (perfection) makes people think of a river. On this side of the river are the troubles of the mind: lobha (wanting), dosa (anger) and moha (ignorance8). On the far side is nibbāna (the end of all troubles). The ten perfections carry a person across. Mind moments. The Pali word for the mind is citta (mind). A citta (mind) lasts one moment. There is a moment of seeing. It goes. There is a moment of hearing. It goes. There is a moment of thinking. It goes. A citta (mind) can be kusala (good) or akusala (bad). All ten perfections are kusala (good) moments of mind. What Anna says. Anna is seven. She knows three Pali words that the Buddha said: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self). What does that mean? Think of a cart. A cart has wheels, a floor and a pole for the ox. Take away the wheels. Take away the floor. Take away the pole. Where is the cart? There is no cart left over. “Cart” is only a name for the parts when they are together. A nun9 named Vajirā, who had learnt from the Buddha, said The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 5

Page 6

that a person is like that. A person is a body and a mind. And the mind is one moment after another. “Anna” is a name for all of that. There is no little Anna inside who stays the same and owns it all. That is anattā (not self). This matters for the perfections. When there is giving, nobody inside does the giving. There is a good moment of mind. It gives, and then it is gone. The old teachers say that a perfection is giving, or patience, or any of the ten, that is not spoilt by wanting, by pride, or by the wrong idea of a self. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) did good without thinking “I am the good one”. Every chapter in this book ends by looking at that. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life 2. energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going 3. truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it 4. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 5. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 6. even-mindedness: having a mind that stays level and calm whatever happens 7. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 8. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 9. nun: a woman who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 6

Page 7

Chapter 1. Dāna (giving) “Na sasassa tilā atthi, na muggā napi taṇḍulā; iminā agginā pakkaṃ, mamaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”: The hare has no sesame, no beans and no rice. Eat me, cooked on this fire, and live on in the forest. (Jātaka 316) Dāna (giving) means giving something away to help someone else. It can be food. It can be a toy. It can be a kind word, or a bit of time. When there is giving, the mind lets go. For that one moment there is no holding on. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a water pot. When a full pot is turned upside down, all the water pours out. The pot keeps none of it back. Sumedha said: give like that pot. Give to everyone who asks, the great and the small and the ones in between, and keep nothing back. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 7

Page 8

the full pot, turned upside down all the water pours out; the pot keeps none back the great the ones in between the small give to everyone who asks “Yathāpi kumbho sampuṇṇo, yassa kassaci adhokato; vamatevudakaṃ nissesaṃ, na tattha parirakkhati”: Like a full pot that is turned upside down: it pours out all its water and keeps none back. (Buddhavaṃsa 2) The story of the wise hare. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a hare. He lived in a forest by a river. He had three friends: a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare was wise, and the three friends listened to him. He told them: do no harm, and give to those who ask. One evening the hare looked up at the moon. It was full. He told his friends that the next day was the uposatha (the holy day), and that if anyone came asking for food, they should give him their own food before they ate. The next day the otter found seven fish. The jackal found some meat and a pot of milk curds. The monkey found ripe mangoes. They put their food by and waited. The hare had nothing but grass, and nobody eats grass. He thought: if someone comes asking, I will give him my own body. Sakka, the king of the devas (heavenly beings1), knew that thought. He wanted to see if it was real. So he came down to the forest dressed as a brahmin2 (a priest), and he went from one friend to the next, asking for food. The otter offered his fish. The jackal offered his meat and curds. The monkey offered his mangoes. Each time the brahmin said he would eat later, and went on. Then he came to the hare. The hare was glad. He told the brahmin to light a fire. The brahmin did. Then the hare shook himself three times, so that any tiny creatures in his fur could get away and not be burnt. And he jumped into the fire. But the fire did not burn him. It felt cool, like cold water. The hare looked round and asked the brahmin why. Then Sakka showed who he really was. He said he had come to test the hare, and that the hare’s gift would be known for ever. He squeezed a mountain in his hand, and with its juice he drew a hare on the moon. The old books say the hare is there still. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 8

Page 9

Three sizes of giving. The old teachers say giving has three sizes. Giving a thing is the small size. Giving a part of one’s own body is the middle size. Giving one’s own life, as the hare did, is the biggest size of all. Anna gives. Anna has two sweets. Her friend has none. Anna gives one away. That is dāna (giving). It is small. But it is the same kind of thing the hare did. Giving starts small, and it grows every time it is done. No one inside. Who gave the sweet? Anna, people say. But look closer. There was a good moment of mind. It saw the friend. It let go of the sweet. It moved the hand. Then that moment was gone, and a new one came. There was no little Anna inside the moment, doing the giving. The giving was done by a kusala citta (good mind). Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self). And the good deed3 is not lost. It is kamma (a deed), and kamma (a deed) brings its fruit later, as a seed brings a fruit. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 2. brahmin: a man of the priestly class in ancient India 3. deed: something done; an act, good or bad The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 9

Page 10

Chapter 2. Sīla (good conduct) “Mātā me sā mahārāja, andhā apariṇāyikā”: Great king, she is my mother. She is blind, and she has no one to lead her. (Jātaka 455) Sīla (good conduct) means not hurting anyone by what one does or says. The Buddha gave five rules for it: 1. not to kill any living being1, not even an ant 2. not to take what is not given 3. not to do wrong with someone else’s husband or wife 4. not to tell lies 5. not to drink alcohol Two helpers. Two things in the mind keep the rules. One is hiri (shame): the mind does not want to do a dirty thing. The other is ottappa (fear of doing wrong): the mind sees what a bad deed2 brings later, and draws back. When these two are there, the rules are kept without any trouble. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a yak. A yak is a big mountain ox with a long, beautiful tail. If its tail gets caught in a bush, the yak will not pull. It would rather die there than tear its tail. Sumedha said: guard good conduct like that, in every life, as the yak guards its tail. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 10

Page 11

the yak it will not pull, and it will not tear its tail the thorn bush its tail is caught sīla (good conduct) is guarded like the yak's tail “Yathāpi camarī vālaṃ, kismiñci paṭilaggitaṃ; upeti maraṇaṃ tattha, na vikopeti vāladhiṃ”: Like the yak whose tail is caught on something: it will die there rather than tear its tail. (Buddhavaṃsa 2) The story of the elephant who looked after his mother. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a great white elephant. He lived in the forest with his mother. His mother was blind. Every day the elephant brought her sweet fruit and lotus3 roots, and he found her cool water. One day a man got lost in the forest. He cried and cried. The elephant heard him and led him out to the road. But the man was not grateful. He went to the king and said: in the forest there is a splendid elephant, fit for a king. The king sent his elephant trainers to catch it. The elephant saw the men coming with ropes. He was very strong. He could have crushed them all. But he thought: if I fight, I will hurt them, and my sīla (good conduct) will be broken. So he stood still and let them tie him up. They took him to the king’s city and put him in a fine stable with sweet food. He would not eat. The king came and asked him why. The elephant said that his mother was blind and alone in the forest, and that nobody was there to feed her. The king was moved. He said: set this great elephant free, who cares for his mother. The elephant went straight back. He filled his trunk with water and sprinkled it over his mother. She thought it was rain. Then he spoke, and she knew that her son had come home. Anna and the ant. There is an ant on the table. Anna could squash it. She does not. She lets it walk away. That is sīla (good conduct). And the ant gets a gift too: it is safe. The Buddha said that a person who does not kill gives safety to every living being. No one inside. Who kept the rule? There was a moment of mind with hiri (shame) and ottappa (fear of doing wrong) in it. It did not move the hand. Then it was gone. Nobody inside Anna keeps the rules in a box. The rules are kept one moment at a time. When the next moment comes, they have to be kept again. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 11

Page 12

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 2. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 3. lotus: a water flower that grows up from the mud and opens clean above the water The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 12

Page 13

Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) The answers are at the back. 1. What did the hare give to the brahmin (the priest)? (a) seven fish (b) ripe mangoes (c) his own body 2. What was Sumedha’s picture for dāna (giving)? (a) a full pot turned upside down (b) a lion (c) a mountain 3. True or false: the fire burnt the hare. 4. Why did the elephant let the king’s men tie him up? (a) he was too weak to fight (b) he did not want to break his sīla (good conduct) (c) he wanted to live in the city 5. Which animal did Sumedha think of for sīla (good conduct)? (a) a monkey (b) a yak that will not tear its tail (c) a quail 6. True or false: hiri (shame) and ottappa (fear of doing wrong) help the mind to keep the rules. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 13

Page 14

Chapter 3. Nekkhamma (letting go) “Ussāvabinduṃ sūriyātape, patitaṃ disvāna saṃvijiṃ”: When I saw a dewdrop fall in the heat of the sun, I was shaken. (Cariyāpiṭaka 3.1) Nekkhamma (letting go) means not chasing after nice things all the time: nice sights, nice sounds, nice smells, nice tastes, nice things to touch. It means being happy with enough. A monk1 lets go of his home. A child can let go of a second piece of cake. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a man locked in a prison for a long time. The man does not love the prison. He does not want to stay. He only looks for the way out. Sumedha said: see every life like that prison, and look for the way out. The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 14

Page 15

the man shut in for a long time he does not love the prison; he only looks for the way out the way out every life is like this prison “Yathā andughare puriso, ciravuttho dukhaṭṭito; na tattha rāgaṃ janesi, muttiṃyeva gavesati”: Like a man long shut in a prison, worn down by suffering: he does not love the place; he looks only for the way out. (Buddhavaṃsa 2) The story of Prince Yudhañjaya. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was a prince named Yudhañjaya. He was the king’s eldest son, and one day he would be king. He had everything a prince could want. One morning he drove out early to the park. The sun was just coming up. On every blade of grass and on every spider’s web there hung drops of dew. They shone like pearls. The prince looked at them and was happy. Then the sun rose higher. The dewdrops grew smaller. One by one they were gone. The prince looked, and his heart was shaken. He thought: these drops were here, and now they are not. Everything is like that. My own life is like that. He went to his mother and father and bowed to them. He asked to leave the palace and live in the forest as a hermit2. They cried. The whole city begged him to stay and be king. But the prince let the kingdom go. He was not angry with his parents, and he did not hate the palace. He only wanted something better than all of it: to become a Buddha. His younger brother went with him, and the two of them lived in the Himalaya mountains. Anna and the second piece. There is cake. Anna has had one piece. It was lovely. There is one piece left. Her mouth wants it. But she is full. She leaves it. That is nekkhamma (letting go). It is a tiny bit of what the prince did. No one inside. The wanting that came for the cake was lobha (wanting). It came. It went. It was not Anna. It was a visitor. When lobha (wanting) is seen as a visitor that comes and goes, it is easier to let it go. Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self). HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER The Ten Perfections for Young Readers · 15
